explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king, says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." To not want means to lack nothing he needs. I spent years in a junk drawer lacking a whole list of things, and light was at the top. David's shepherd leaves nothing off the list.

David, Israel's king, never mentions earning anything here. He says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." The shepherd supplies what he needs, and sheep don't punch a time clock. It's close to the other word, but the verse is about lacking nothing.

That one sounds close, friend. David, Israel's king, says, "I shall not want," which means he lacks nothing he needs. He isn't talking about keeping hold of things. He's talking about a shepherd who has him covered.

David says, "He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters." Lying down and quiet water. Nobody in that picture is sweating. After my drawer years, I can tell you that sounds like a vacation.

Nobody in this picture is hustling. David is lying down in green pastures, and he's being led beside quiet waters. The words are about lying down and being led. If you came for a grind, this verse sends you home with a nap.
Danger isn't in this verse. David says, "He leads me beside quiet waters," and the word is quiet. The scary part of the song comes in a different verse. Here the grass is green and the water is calm.

David says, "He restores my soul." Restore means to bring back, to set right again. I know a little about being worn down, friend, and getting set right again is a gift. This part of the care goes deeper than grass and water.
David doesn't say the LORD tests his soul. He says, "He restores my soul." Restoring means bringing something back to how it should be. This verse is about care, not a pop quiz.
Nobody is putting David's soul on a scale here. He says, "He restores my soul." That means bringing it back and setting it right. No scale, just a shepherd who cares.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: David says, "He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name." That's the reason he gives, word for word. He doesn't say the LORD guides him for some other cause. I'll leave it right where David leaves it.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: A shepherd and a flock sound like a natural pair, friend. But David's reason is a different one. He says, "He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name." The words are His name, not His flock.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: David never mentions land in this line. He says, "He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name." The reason is the LORD's name. Keep an eye on the last words of a verse, because that's where the answer is hiding.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: David says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." That's his reason. The valley didn't change, but he isn't walking it alone. Walking a dark hallway by yourself is one thing, and walking it with somebody beside you is another.
David doesn't lean on his own strength here. He says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." His reason is the LORD beside him. Even for a king, that's the answer he gives.
David never says the valley is short. He calls it "the valley of the shadow of death" and says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." The reason is who's with him, not how far there is to go.

David says, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me." A big stick in a dark valley could scare you, but David finds comfort in it. I think that's because the shepherd is holding it. Whatever else is in that valley, the comfort is real.
The verse says the opposite, friend. David says, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me." They comfort him, right there in the valley of the shadow of death. So this one is true.
David says, "You prepare a table before me." The picture is a host setting a table for a guest. I've set a few tables in my day, and I know getting ready for someone is a way of saying they matter.
No tent in this verse, friend. David says, "You prepare a table before me." It's a table, which is what a host sets out for a guest.
Nobody's being tucked in here. David says, "You prepare a table before me." A table is where a host welcomes a guest. A bed would be a different verse.

The verse says the opposite. David says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." In the presence of them, not far away from them. The enemies are right there, and the table gets set anyway.
Right, friend. David says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." Not far from them, but in their presence. The enemies can see the table, and it's still set for David.

David says, "my cup overflows." A cup that spills over is holding more than it needs, and I think that's the picture he wants you to see. He's got more than enough, and he knows where it came from. That's a good thing to be able to say.

I've knocked over a whole bowl of dough in my day, and that was careless. But David isn't describing a spill. He says, "my cup overflows," right after the LORD has prepared a table for him. I think the picture is more than enough, not a mess.

Nobody is rushing David here. He's at a table the LORD prepared for him, and he says, "my cup overflows." A cup spilling over is a picture of more than enough. It isn't a picture of a host in a hurry.
David says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life." They follow him, and not just on a good day. It says all the days. That's a lot of days for good things to keep up.
That's a nice pair, friend, but it isn't David's pair. He says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life." The two things following him are goodness and mercy.
Those two are good things to have, but David names others. He says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life." Goodness and mercy are the ones trailing behind him.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: David ends with, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever." Dwell means he stays there, and forever means no end date. After all those years in a drawer I was waiting to be let out. David's last line is about being welcomed in to stay.
David doesn't name a city anywhere in this song. His last line is, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever." The place he names is the LORD's house. No street address needed.
David doesn't name any land in his closing line. He says, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever." The home he looks forward to is the LORD's house, and the song ends there.
